How does a human keep self-improving? 2 Action 2.1 Robotics 2.1.1 The policy emits a position; the servo stack supplies the force The policy issues a position. The servo stack turns position into force. 2.1.2 Compliance can be added beneath the policy, in hardware, torque, or target Passive compliance puts the spring in the hardware. Impedance control puts the spring in the torque command. Admittance control puts the spring in the position target. Only a minority of policies emit something other than position. 2.1.3 Action chunking decouples control rate from inference rate, at the cost of blindness mid-chunk and seams between chunks The policy is blind for the executed part of each chunk. Consecutive chunks must be joined. 2.1.4 Token or number, absolute or delta, the representation changes how the position is encoded Discrete heads inherit the language prior; continuous heads give precision and multimodality. Delta actions pool across embodiments; absolute targets stop error compounding. 2.2 Biology 2.2.1 The motor neuron integrates cortical, brainstem, and reflex drive into one command 2.2.2 The population firing rate of a muscle’s motor neurons is translated into effort 2.2.3 Opposing muscle pairs set torque and stiffness separately 2.2.4 Slip during a grasp is caught by a reflex that corrects grip force, with no position in the loop 2.3 Inspiration 2.3.1 Use compliance so the world supplies what the policy would otherwise compute 2.3.2 On the position-controlled arms most policies run on, keep the position output, add a stiffness beneath it, and let touch set where to yield and how hard to press Touch tells the controller where to yield and how hard to press. 3 Touch 3.1 Robotics 3.1.1 No sensor family matches human skin on resolution, speed, and force at once Touch rarely extends beyond the fingertips. 3.1.2 Policies now take touch as an input, but data and control rate hold it back Touch enters the policy as an extra image or as learned tokens. Cost, standardization, scale, and speed still hold touch back. 3.2 Biology 3.2.1 Four receptor classes encode touch in spike timing A mechanoreceptor reports only through spike timing. Tactile percepts arise from combining the four receptor classes. 3.2.2 Successive contacts build an object representation beyond geometry S1 estimates the surface under one fingertip. Parietal cortex assembles the whole object from many contacts. Vision and touch converge into one object representation. 3.2.3 Tactile reflexes correct grip within about 75 ms, faster than any visual correction 3.2.4 The brain predicts touch and acts on the discrepancy 3.2.5 Descending control suppresses predictable and irrelevant tactile channels 3.3 Inspiration 3.3.1 Represent touch as a force field first, and let it drive compliance control 3.3.2 Train the model to predict the tactile consequence of each command 3.3.3 Probe actively to test hypotheses about properties that cannot be seen 4 Vision 4.1 Robotics 4.1.1 The pretraining objective decides what the tokens keep Self-supervised encoders predict the input, in pixel space or in latent space. Caption alignment buys semantics but never asks for geometry. 4.1.2 The VLM or video world-model backbone acts as an extended vision encoder 4.1.3 Current vision stacks are slow, blind to velocity, and miss fine detail Policies act on one stale observation for up to seconds. Single frames carry no velocity. Fine detail is lost. 4.2 Biology 4.2.1 The retina compresses before transmitting, and recognition and action get separate streams Recognition and control get separate streams with different codes. 4.2.2 The dorsal stream is modeled as a bank of parallel channels, one per class of action 4.2.3 Vision selects one object, holds it on the fovea, and tracks its motion 4.2.4 Each dorsal channel re-expresses visual information toward the frame its effector needs The frame follows the effector: eye for gaze, head for near space, hand for reach and grasp. The transform is a population code built from gain fields. 4.2.5 Vision is slow, so the brain acts on a prediction and corrects it later The eye moved: an exact command. The body moved: a command plus limb dynamics. The world moved: no command, only observation and priors. 4.3 Inspiration 4.3.1 Add a fast streaming encoder for control beside the slow one for recognition Feed a camera-rate encoder straight into the reactive policy head. Distill the fast encoder from video models, then train it on control losses. 4.3.2 Read the numbers and the decisions an action unit needs off one encoded frame Encourage the model to emit more of each unit’s parameters directly from vision. Answer the unit’s decisions with parallel typed experts over one encoded frame. 4.3.3 Move the camera to see better, and train across viewpoints Move the camera to see better. Give the model its camera pose, and train it to use it. 5 Is the cerebellum the brain’s world model? 5.1 Robotics 5.1.1 World Action Models train the policy under a world-prediction loss How prediction is coupled to action decides what reaches the policy. The video branch that supplies the prior is also the source of the open problems. 5.1.2 Test-time adaptation stores recent experience in a latent, in temporary weights, or in the context A latent compresses recent experience into one vector. Temporary weights hold more than a latent can. The context window holds the raw history. 5.2 Biology 5.2.1 A three-synapse, very wide circuit predicts before the senses report 5.2.2 Error signals recalibrate the cerebellum locally and fast The climbing fiber delivers the error to the synapses that made the prediction. Wiring gives the error its direction, and the expansion keeps the correction local. One error produces a brief correction; repeated errors consolidate over days to weeks. 5.2.3 The prediction amends the action in flight or returns to cortex Descending, the prediction amends the action in flight. Ascending, the prediction returns to the cortex that issued the command. The cerebellum also sets timing and reaches the reward system. 5.3 Inspiration 5.3.1 Consult the predictor as a tool when it is slow 5.3.2 Run the predictor in the loop when it is fast 5.3.3 Make the predictor shallow, wide, and sparse, so it is fast and adapts at test time 5.3.4 Tag every joint and sensor with a body-part embedding so the map transfers 6 Planning and command: how the brain divides what a VLA does in one network 6.1 Robotics 6.1.1 A VLA is a backbone plus action head 6.1.2 Three training stages shape the VLA, and none writes deployment experience back Pretraining imitates demonstrations, and demonstrations are scarce. Supervised fine-tuning adapts the policy to one robot and keeps the imitation objective. Reinforcement learning is the only stage at which success enters the objective. 6.1.3 A planner decomposes the task into subgoals for a fast executor 6.1.4 A multimodal large language model writes the policy as code 6.1.5 Experience enters the model in context, as skills, or in the weights, and no loop yet runs without a human Past experience reaches the model by three routes. Automating the loop is the open part. 6.2 Biology 6.2.1 Prefrontal cortex sets the goal, SMA holds the action units, and ACC keeps the place 6.2.2 Motor cortex holds sensor-tuned primitives, and a competition among premotor candidates chooses which to compose 6.2.3 The cerebellum’s forecast amends the current unit and times the next 6.2.4 Practice turns the composition into a habit, selected by dopamine and consolidated offline 6.3 Inspiration 6.3.1 Let the model compose action units from reusable primitives and verify each at its boundary 6.3.2 Treat each primitive as a parameterized template 6.3.3 Let the model run each unit by Cartesian control or by a reactive policy head 6.3.4 Add a consolidation agent that graduates proven primitives from code into weights Consolidation first cleans the script, keeping the shortest sequence that is grounded and explained. Each measurement then graduates from code into a typed function the model answers directly. In the end the policy head runs the primitive end to end, and only the test stays explicit. 6.3.5 Design the next architecture so that primitives are experts routed by the plan and share embeddings 6.3.6 Add a practice agent that rehearses weak skills and tests what consolidation wrote It picks the most valuable tasks and practices their weakest unit. It treats each record as a hypothesis and runs the trial that would refute it. 6.3.7 Mastering a new skill rests on judging which direction moves it closer to success 7 Conclusion One model composes the new task from verified primitives. Compliance and touch let the world supply what the policy would otherwise compute. A reactive policy head and a streaming encoder make the motion fast and continuous. A predictor beside the model forecasts the consequence of each action and trains itself. Perception moves from explicit code into typed functions, then into the weights. The robot should practice and sense on its own initiative. Limitations and outlook. References License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.02510v1 [cs.RO] 02 Nov 2026 Neuro Inspired Robotics: What Robot Learning Can Borrow from the Sensorimotor Brain Ruihan Zhang † † thanks: ruihanzhang2015@gmail.com Davy Deng † † thanks: davy@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT Abstract Robot policies still fail at everyday manipulation: an unfamiliar task, an object never held before, a scene that changes mid-motion, a skill that should improve with use. They fail despite pretraining on over a million trajectories, pooled from dozens of robots at great expense, while a child acquires all of these abilities within a few years of learning from a single body. This survey argues that the gap is one of design, and proposes designs for the next generation of robot models, drawn from how the nervous system solves the same problems. From the body we take compliance: the policy commands stiffness alongside position, so the controller yields where the task allows and presses where it must, which greatly lowers the demand for precise position output. From the visual system, where a fast pathway for action runs in parallel with the slow pathway for recognition, we take a dedicated fast vision system for motor behavior: it precomputes the quantities the policy needs and drives a reactive policy at camera rate. From the cerebellum we take a predictor beside the policy that forecasts the consequence of each command and recalibrates from its own error. From motor cortex we take a single model that composes action units from primitives, verifies each at a sensory boundary, practices the weakest unit with a hypothesis in mind, and reasons each attempt closer to the goal. Proven primitives are then consolidated from code into weights, so they run fluently and respond quickly the next time. Together these describe a robot that acts on its own initiative, the basis of deployment and recursive self-improvement, and we offer each proposal as a hypothesis to be tested. Keywords: robot learning; embodied AI; neuroscience; biological priors; vision-language-action models; world models; compliance control; tactile sensing; motor primitives; recursive self-improvement acquired every one of these skills from a single body over a single childhood. In contrast, robot policies trained on over a million trajectories pooled across dozens of robots still fail at tasks this simple ( Figure 1 ) [ 296 , 42 , 210 ] . Scale alone cannot explain the gap, because the child never saw more than seven years of data. The difference is in how the nervous system is organized, which makes the child more dexterous, more intelligent, and able to keep improving. This survey asks how that sensorimotor skill develops and which parts of the design robotics can borrow. It is built around three questions: 1a 1b 2a 2b 3a 3b Human behavior Common limitations of current robot policies Unfamiliar task Sudden change Keep improving Figure 1: A child has three abilities that current robot policies lack. Top: a boy opens an unfamiliar drawer on the first try, while a policy finds no training handle to copy. Middle: a girl catches a flying toy, while a robot is still reasoning about shape and coordinates when the toy lands. Bottom: the boy’s piano playing improves with days of practice, while a robot never trained on the piano cannot learn it or improve over time, because its learning stopped the day it was deployed. How does a human solve a task it has never seen? Never from scratch. A policy trained end to end has nothing to copy when the scene falls outside its training data ( Figure 1 ). The brain instead uses reasoning to split the task into a sequence of action units and composes each from a small repertoire of primitives such as reach, orient, and grasp, each a verifiable goal and an action plan, so an unfamiliar drawer becomes reach, grasp, and pull on the first try. Each unit ends at a sensory event, the hand closing on the handle, and the brain checks for it before releasing the next. When the check fails, it reasons to the cause and revises the plan ( Section 6 ). Why does a human act so fast? Robotics debates how to pair a large reasoning model, powerful but slow, with a small action policy, fast but shallow, so the system is quick, capable, and still fits on the GPU a robot can carry. The brain escapes the trade-off by keeping deliberation off the path from sensing to action. A second visual stream, largely separate from the one that recognizes objects, guides the next movement ( Section 4 ). Its commands can be coarse because the body is compliant: the controller only decides where motion must be exact and where external forces can carry it ( Section 2 ). Touch corrects a slipping grip by reflex within a hundred milliseconds, before vision registers the slip ( Section 3 ). And on the leading account of the cerebellum, a predictor forecasts each command’s consequence before the sensors report it, so the response is ready when the world catches up ( Section 5 ). How does a human keep self-improving? A robot policy is trained once before deployment, and naive fine-tuning risks erasing what it knew [ 262 , 212 ] . The brain keeps learning after deployment, on two timescales. Within minutes the predictor recalibrates to a new tool or a heavier door ( Section 5 ). Over weeks, practice concentrates on the step that still fails, dopamine scores each attempt and keeps what worked, and consolidation during rest and sleep turns the result into an action primitive that runs with little deliberation ( Section 6 ). Once consolidated, a skill resists interference from the next, so learning adds without erasing. The survey follows the flow of information through a motor system. It begins with the modalities that carry it, action as output ( Section 2 ) and touch and vision as inputs ( Sections 3 and 4 ), and where brain and robot differ on each. Two models connect them. One predicts the consequence of a command: the cerebellum in the brain, the world model in robotics ( Section 5 ). The other decides what to do: the motor hierarchy from prefrontal to motor cortex in the brain, vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action policies (VLAs) in robotics ( Section 6 ). Each chapter reviews where robotics stands, how the brain solves the same problem, and what to build. Evolution has run this experiment for hundreds of millions of years, and we hope its principles point toward robots that are intelligent, swift, and able to improve themselves. 2 Action Figure 2: The slot walls supply the rod’s trajectory. The hand pushes along the slot and yields across it, so the walls shape the path and the controller has far less of the curve to compute. In biology, action leaves the nervous system as spike trains on motor axons; in a robot, it leaves the policy as a vector of numbers. What the limb then does is a transformation of that signal by what lies downstream: muscle, tendon, and joint on one side, servo loops and motors on the other. The deepest difference is what the signal names. Robots command position , where the limb should end up [ 50 ] ; the nervous system’s final command is effort , how hard each muscle pulls [ 442 , 103 ] . The brain also sets stiffness per task, deciding what must be precise and what can be left to the environment, whereas in a position-controlled robot the stiffness is set once by the servo gains, outside the policy’s reach [ 53 , 115 ] . So a robot must compute every detail of a trajectory, while a human lets the environment supply part of it ( Figure 2 ). We first survey how robotics handles action ( Section 2.1 ), then how biology does it ( Section 2.2 ), and finally draw the inspirations ( Section 2.3 ). 2.1 Robotics Action, what a policy emits, is the boundary between the learned policy and the hand-tuned controllers that drive the motors. In the robotics literature the quantity that crosses it is nearly always a position, handed to a fixed servo stack that turns it into force ( Section 2.1.1 ). The remaining choices concern only how the position is delivered: as a single target or a chunk ( Section 2.1.3 ), and as a discrete token or a continuous number ( Section 2.1.4 ). 2.1.1 The policy emits a position; the servo stack supplies the force The policy issues a position. In nearly all imitation-learning and VLA work the policy outputs a position: joint angles, as in ACT and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 450 , 42 ] , or an end-effector pose, as in Diffusion Policy and OpenVLA [ 70 , 210 ] . It runs at 5–50 Hz [ 70 , 42 , 209 ] , hands each target to the servo stack and moves on to the next observation; how the target becomes torque is neither observed by the policy nor represented in its output. The servo stack turns position into force. The conversion is a cascade of nested feedback loops, each output the setpoint of the next, faster loop [ 357 , 173 ] . The policy’s position target enters a joint PD servo, at up to 1 kHz, that turns position and velocity error into torque via fixed gains [ 114 ] . That torque drives a torque loop, which sets the motor current the driver regulates at a still higher rate. This has two costs. A target is correct only under the gains it was trained with, so a policy transfers poorly across actuators unless their response is modeled or randomized [ 174 , 308 ] . Modeling fits the real actuator’s command-to-torque response and places it in the simulator; randomizing varies gains, latency, friction, and motor strength from one training episode to the next, so the policy cannot rely on any single response and must infer the one it faces from proprioceptive feedback. And the servo cannot tell intended contact from an obstacle: it pushes with a torque that grows with the error until something yields or a limit trips. Contact-rich behavior must therefore be restored beneath the policy, through force sensing [ 247 ] , compliant hardware [ 320 ] , or torque limits [ 145 ] . 2.1.2 Compliance can be added beneath the policy, in hardware, torque, or target Compliance is the inverse of stiffness, the displacement yielded per unit of applied force, and a compliance controller regulates that relation rather than position alone. The robot then behaves like a chosen spring and damper about its target, so a push displaces it by a predictable amount and a contact error produces a bounded force [ 161 , 357 ] . Three schemes supply the spring, and they differ in where it lives. Passive compliance puts the spring in the hardware. The remote-center-compliance wrist arranges elastic elements so that a peg touching the chamfer of a hole is steered into alignment by the contact forces themselves, with no sensing or computation [ 410 ] . Series elastic actuators place a spring between motor and load, so that motor position becomes a force command through the spring’s deflection [ 320 ] . Passive compliance acts at the speed of physics, but its stiffness is fixed once, at design time. Impedance control puts the spring in the torque command. The controller measures the joint’s displacement and velocity from its target, computes the force a virtual spring and damper would exert there, and commands the motors to produce it [ 161 ] . Stiffness and damping become numbers the controller can change between tasks or within a movement. The price is that the actuators must deliver a commanded torque, through backdrivable transmissions, series elastic actuators, or joint torque sensing, as in the KUKA iiwa and Franka [ 408 , 8 , 114 ] . Conventional industrial arms do not: friction and reflected inertia in their high-ratio gearboxes make motor current a poor estimate of external force [ 145 ] . Admittance control puts the spring in the position target. On a stiff position-servoed arm the relation runs the other way. A wrist force sensor measures the contact, the controller computes the displacement a virtual spring would suffer under that force, and it shifts the position target by that amount, so the arm yields even though the servo beneath it never outputs a torque [ 357 ] . This is how compliance is retrofitted to a position stack, and it is the form the correction of Section 2.3.2 takes. Only a minority of policies emit something other than position. Compliance control is well established beneath the policy, yet few policies emit anything but position. The exceptions are scattered: a few reinforcement-learned locomotion policies output joint torques directly [ 67 ] , a few manipulation policies output the force to apply along contact directions [ 237 ] , and a few emit an impedance target, a position together with the stiffness at which to hold it [ 161 , 164 ] . 2.1.3 Action chunking decouples control rate from inference rate, at the cost of blindness mid-chunk and seams between chunks The policy is blind for the executed part of each chunk. Action chunking has the policy predict a chunk of H H future targets from one observation rather than one target per step [ 450 , 70 ] . Fewer decisions per episode means less compounding error, and the control rate is no longer capped by inference speed: a VLA forward pass takes 50–300 ms while joint servos expect targets at 50 Hz or more, so a chunk of 0.5–2 s at 10–50 Hz lets the robot execute one chunk while the next is computed [ 210 , 42 ] . The cost is that a mid-chunk disturbance is answered only by the servo stack of Section 2.1.1 , which holds the commanded positions against it whether or not that is appropriate. Consecutive chunks must be joined. Each chunk is generated from an observation that is stale by the inference time, and nothing forces it to agree with the chunk still executing, so the boundary can produce a discontinuity. Temporal ensembling averages the overlapping predictions of successive chunks [ 450 ] ; bidirectional decoding samples several candidates and keeps the one most consistent with the executed prefix [ 250 ] ; real-time chunking freezes the actions that will execute during inference and generates the rest conditioned on them, with a soft mask so that later actions stay free to respond to the new observation [ 43 ] . 2.1.4 Token or number, absolute or delta, the representation changes how the position is encoded Discrete heads inherit the language prior; continuous heads give precision and multimodality. Binning each action dimension into a fixed vocabulary lets a pretrained VLM emit actions by next-token prediction [ 49 , 210 ] , but a chunk binned step by step is mostly redundant, since successive samples of a smooth trajectory are nearly equal; FAST compresses chunks with a discrete cosine transform before byte-pair encoding [ 310 ] . Continuous heads instead regress the numbers directly: L 1 L_{1} regression is cheapest but collapses several valid actions onto a single compromise value [ 70 ] , and diffusion or flow matching recovers the full distribution over several denoising steps [ 159 , 70 , 42 ] . π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0 \pi_{0} -FAST put the two heads on a shared backbone and isolate exactly this trade-off [ 42 , 310 ] . Delta actions pool across embodiments; absolute targets stop error compounding. Delta end-effector actions [ 48 , 294 , 210 ] are relative to the current pose, hence invariant to initial configuration and small enough to tokenize well, which is why cross-embodiment datasets favor them [ 296 ] . But each delta is applied to wherever the arm actually is, so a lag or slip shifts every later target with it [ 70 ] . Absolute targets, joint angles in ACT and π 0 \pi_{0} or poses in Diffusion Policy [ 450 , 42 , 70 ] , live in a fixed frame, so each error is corrected at the next step rather than carried forward [ 70 ] . But that frame is tied to one body: joint angles to one arm’s kinematics, poses to one base placement. 2.2 Biology We define action in biology as the output of the motor neurons of the spinal cord, the final common path through which every descending and reflex influence must pass [ 347 ] . The brain’s decisions arrive there as synaptic input, and what leaves is a train of action potentials that the muscle turns into movement [ 197 , 442 ] . 2.2.1 The motor neuron integrates cortical, brainstem, and reflex drive into one command Every alpha motor neuron receives a voluntary stream from cortex, a postural and locomotor stream from the brainstem, and a reflex stream from sensors in the muscle itself, and its output depends largely on their sum. The cortical stream is on the order of 10 6 10^{6} corticospinal axons [ 226 , 225 ] , most ending on spinal interneurons, that drive on the order of 10 5 10^{5} motor neurons [ 378 ] . The brainstem stream carries posture and the go and speed commands for locomotion; the rhythm itself comes from central pattern generators, in the spinal cord for walking and running and in the brainstem for breathing and chewing, which produce it on their own [ 139 , 351 ] . The reflex stream closes fast loops that never wait on the brain: the spinal stretch reflex returns a limb toward its load within roughly 30 ms, with a cortical component following 20–30 ms later [ 261 ] , and the grip reflex of Section 2.2.4 tightens the fingers on a slipping object. The action that leaves the nervous system is therefore the sum of the brain’s decision, locally generated rhythm, and sensory feedback. 2.2.2 The population firing rate of a muscle’s motor neurons is translated into effort More drive onto a muscle’s motor pool recruits more of its neurons and fires each faster [ 153 , 273 ] . The muscle turns that firing into a contraction that is its smoothed copy [ 306 ] , so the command is an effort. That force rises with the muscle’s stretch over much of its working range, falls with its shortening speed [ 158 , 132 ] , and acts through a lever arm that changes with joint angle [ 281 ] , so the same firing gives a different torque at every posture, outside neural control. The stretch dependence makes an active muscle a spring, and the limb settles wherever its pull and the world agree. 2.2.3 Opposing muscle pairs set torque and stiffness separately Muscles come in opposing pairs, one pulling each way across a joint, so every joint is held between two springs. Two drives per joint thus set two quantities at once [ 160 ] . Their difference is the net torque ( Figure 3 , left): flexor pull above extensor pull flexes the elbow, the reverse extends it, and equal pulls leave it balanced. Their sum sets the stiffness ( Figure 3 , right): co-contracting both muscles leaves the pose and the net torque unchanged, but the elbow that was easy to push aside under light co-contraction now resists the same push under strong co-contraction. Torque and stiffness are therefore two largely independent commands sent through one pair of muscles. Figure 3: Opposing muscles set torque and stiffness separately. The difference of flexor and extensor pull sets the net torque, and their sum sets the stiffness at the same pose. 2.2.4 Slip during a grasp is caught by a reflex that corrects grip force, with no position in the loop During a grasp, grip force follows the motor pool’s firing with a short delay [ 187 , 306 ] , and the whole task is specified in that quantity. The precision grip regulates the ratio of grip force to load force, holds it a fixed margin above the slip limit, and raises it 74 ± 9 74\pm 9 ms after a micro-slip [ 189 ] , with no positional quantity anywhere in the specification. The slip itself is read from the skin’s mechanoreceptors, whose classes and the signals they combine into a slip event are described in Section 3.2.1 . The correction is a reflex rather than a decision: a sudden pull on the held object triggers the same grip increase within about 70 ms, before any voluntary response [ 192 ] , and anesthetizing the fingertips delays and weakens it, so the loop is closed mainly by those cutaneous afferents rather than by muscle sense [ 191 ] ; Section 3 takes up what the loop should look like in a robot. 2.3 Inspiration From the two subsections above we draw two lessons for the policy interface. The first is that compliance control matters because it lets the world supply parameters the policy would otherwise have to compute ( Section 2.3.1 ). The second is our proposal for achieving it on the arms most policies run on, which accept only position targets: keep the position output and add a stiffness beneath it, with a touch sensor measuring the contact so the controller can take from it where to yield and how hard to press, moving the position target beneath the policy ( Section 2.3.2 ). 2.3.1 Use compliance so the world supplies what the policy would otherwise compute Consider carrying a rod through a curved slot ( Figure 2 ). A robot with only position commands has to perceive the precise shape of the whole curve, and any error at contact becomes uncontrolled force through a stiff servo. A human does not track the curve. The hand pushes with high stiffness along the slot and low stiffness across it, and lets the board do the shaping: as long as the push is roughly along the slot, the wrist tolerates some wobble, and whatever the wall presents is fine, because the hand yields to it. The same holds when a yielding wrist scrubs a bumpy surface ( Figure 4 ). The controller’s only job is to choose which axes to hold and which to yield; the curve of the slot and the height of each bump arrive through contact for free. Figure 4: Contact supplies the surface detail. A yielding wrist and a soft towel follow the bumps, so the controller computes fewer corrections. 2.3.2 On the position-controlled arms most policies run on, keep the position output, add a stiffness beneath it, and let touch set where to yield and how hard to press We propose that the policy, like the muscle pair of Figure 3 , command a stiffness alongside its target, and that the stiffness be realized beneath it: by impedance control where the joints deliver torque, and by admittance on the position-controlled arms most policies run on, where even Adaptive Compliance Policy had to recover its stiffness through a wrist force sensor [ 164 ] . We take the position-controlled arm as the main case and let touch set where to yield and how hard to press. Touch tells the controller where to yield and how hard to press. On a position-controlled arm we propose adding the stiffness as admittance ( Section 2.1.2 ): a touch sensor measures the contact and the controller moves the position target in response. Against a hard wall, the direction of the sensed force is the direction to yield in, and the rest of the commanded motion goes through unchanged. Against a soft object, the magnitude decides when to stop closing. This rule can be written as code by a language model, as in Code as Policies [ 239 ] , or it can be learned. OmniTacTune [ 437 ] keeps the visual policy frozen and adds a small residual network, trained by reinforcement on the real robot, that reads the tactile signal and corrects the end-effector target while each chunk executes, with the residual scaled to 5–15% of the base action. It raises success on contact-rich tasks from 5–40% to 85–100% within 40–80 minutes of training, on an arm that never outputs a force. 3 Touch Figure 5: Touch alone finds the handle and opens the door. With eyes closed the hand feels its way to the handle, turns it and pushes the door open; in the dark a camera has nothing to offer. A human can find a door handle in the dark and open the door without a single glance ( Figure 5 ). Most current robot policies cannot, because they rely on vision [ 42 , 123 , 255 ] . One might argue that, with the lights on, vision could cover what touch does, but the human evidence says otherwise: with anesthetized fingertips and the hand in plain view, subjects still pick up some objects, yet they apply excessive, poorly scaled forces and drop others [ 191 , 276 , 21 ] . Beyond empirical evidence, a first-principles view says the same. Touch supplies the force in Newton’s second law, F = m ​ a F=ma ; vision sees only displacement, velocity, and acceleration, the right-hand side, and can infer force from them only indirectly. A robot that senses only motion sees the effect of every interaction and must guess its cause, and that cause is what physical intelligence must reason about. This section examines how humans use touch and what robotics can learn from it. 3.1 Robotics Tactile sensing has recently attracted growing attention as an input modality for robot learning [ 255 ] . We first discuss sensors and then how the policy consumes their signal. 3.1.1 No sensor family matches human skin on resolution, speed, and force at once Every robotic touch sensor is a physical filter. The transduction principle fixes what the skin can resolve in space, how fast it responds, and which components of force it reports, and no current family scores well on all three [ 85 , 255 , 424 ] . Table 1 shows the pattern: camera-based pads resolve tens of microns, piezoelectric films catch kilohertz transients but are blind to steady pressure, and the cheapest arrays read normal force only [ 85 , 165 , 373 ] . Durability is a further limit. Touch sensors sit on the part of the robot built to collide with the world, yet the soft elastomer that makes a sensor sensitive wears out long before the electronics beneath it [ 220 , 37 ] . Touch rarely extends beyond the fingertips. Most sensorized hands carry touch only at the fingertips, as caps or gripper pads, and leave the phalanges and palm bare [ 220 , 255 ] . Even at the tip, the sensor covers the pad and not the sides of the fingers that steer chopsticks and scissors [ 85 , 424 ] . Whole-hand skins remain rare: the scalable ones read normal force only [ 367 ] , and shear-capable coverage of palm and fingers exists in a few research hands [ 379 , 451 ] . 3.1.2 Policies now take touch as an input, but data and control rate hold it back Touch enters the policy as an extra image or as learned tokens. The design choice is how the tactile signal is represented. Because vision-based sensors emit images, the simplest approach treats the tactile image as an additional camera view and reuses the vision encoder [ 149 ] . Touch-specific pretraining improves on this borrowed encoder, either through self-supervised learning on tactile video or through contrastive alignment of touch with vision and language [ 155 , 425 ] . Other policies learn tactile tokens of their own: a point cloud from piezoresistive pads [ 169 ] , a single token from the force history [ 170 ] , latent tokens from a dedicated tactile corpus [ 288 ] , or a few tokens compressing the tactile history [ 404 ] . Cost, standardization, scale, and speed still hold touch back. Tactile sensors are expensive and wear quickly, so most demonstrations are collected without them. Each sensor family emits a different signal, an image, a three-axis force, or a pressure array, so data from different platforms cannot be pooled without a learned shared latent space [ 108 , 305 ] . Tactile corpora are therefore orders of magnitude smaller than video [ 432 , 288 ] . Finally, policies run at camera rate, 10–60 Hz, and miss the hundreds-of-hertz transients that signal events such as slip ( Table 1 ). 3.2 Biology 3.2.1 Four receptor classes encode touch in spike timing Figure 6: Slowly adapting (SA) afferents report steady pressure and rapidly adapting (RA) ones report change, so the four classes split what touch carries. The traces are schematic responses to a ramp-and-hold skin indentation: SA afferents sustain firing during the hold, RA afferents respond transiently during pressing and release, and SA2 afferents also fire at a low rate before contact, driven by resting skin stretch. RA afferents can also fire during ongoing motion or vibration. Spike counts and timing are illustrative rather than measured; responses depend on the stimulus and afferent [ 194 , 2 ] . A mechanoreceptor reports only through spike timing. Touch starts in the skin. Buried at different depths are the endings of sensory nerve fibers, most ending in a specialized structure of tissue: the mechanoreceptors [ 186 , 194 , 2 ] . When the capsule deforms, the nerve ending fires brief, stereotyped electrical pulses called spikes. A spike cannot be made bigger to say “more”; a stronger press makes the ending fire sooner and more often, so everything a fiber reports is carried in when its spikes come and how often [ 3 , 194 ] ( Figure 6 ). Tactile percepts arise from combining the four receptor classes. A receptor’s wrapping and depth set two properties: how large a patch of skin it listens to, and whether it reports steady contact (slowly adapting, SA) or only change (rapidly adapting, RA). The four combinations give the four classes in Table 2 : SA1 reports sustained pressure and fine shape, RA1 the onset of movement, SA2 skin stretch and force direction, and RA2 high-frequency vibration. None of them reports a tactile feeling on its own. Texture, weight, and slip each arise from combining the four channels [ 188 ] . When a held glass begins to slide, RA1 afferents fire the most reliable burst at the onset of the slip, with RA2 and SA1 afferents contributing, while the grip force itself has not changed [ 189 ] : a burst of change with no change in squeeze signals slip. The pairing of SA2 afferents with Ruffini endings is disputed, since the human fingertip holds few such endings [ 303 ] . Figure 6 uses the same codes. 3.2.2 Successive contacts build an object representation beyond geometry S1 estimates the surface under one fingertip. Discriminative-touch signals from a fingertip reach the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) through the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway ( Figure 8 ) [ 197 ] . The input is dense, roughly 17,000 tactile afferents for the glabrous skin of the hand [ 186 , 78 ] , and S1 turns it into a first estimate of the surface under each fingertip: area 2 integrates cutaneous input with finger posture to recover the curvature and orientation of the surface in contact [ 197 ] . Parietal cortex assembles the whole object from many contacts. From S1 the signal passes to the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) and on to posterior parietal cortex, where processing moves from individual skin contacts to the object. Parietal cortex relates each contact to hand and arm posture, placing it in space, and so combines touches made by different fingers at different times into an estimate of the object’s three-dimensional form [ 197 ] . Vision and touch converge into one object representation. Tactile and visual shape processing converge in regions such as the lateral occipital tactile-visual area (LOtv), which responds to objects explored by touch as well as those seen [ 11 ] . The two estimates are weighted by their reliability: clear vision dominates, and touch gains weight as visual information becomes uncertain [ 104 ] . The result is one object representation that combines visible geometry with properties only contact reveals, such as weight, texture, and compliance ( Figure 7 ). Figure 7: Vision and touch build a single object model, and each sense fills in what the other cannot. Vision covers the visible surfaces, while touch supplies weight, texture, slipperiness, and compliance, and explores the occluded back. 3.2.3 Tactile reflexes correct grip within about 75 ms, faster than any visual correction Figure 8: Three neurons carry a fingertip signal to primary somatosensory cortex (S1), a chain short enough to leave time for a tactile correction within about 75 ms. The first-order neuron ascends on the same side through the spinal dorsal column to the cuneate nucleus of the medulla; the second-order neuron crosses there and ascends to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamus; the third-order neuron projects to S1 on the side opposite the stimulated hand. Each line ends in a dot at its synapse, and the legend colors mark the three cell bodies. Other branches and circuits are omitted [ 197 ] . Touch does not have to wait for a full object representation before it acts, because tactile signals reach the motor system along two pathways of different speed. The reflex pathway runs through the spinal cord and brainstem, or through the chain of Figure 8 to S1 and the neighboring motor cortex: when a held object begins to slip, grip force rises 74 ± 9 74\pm 9 ms later, before the slip reaches awareness [ 189 , 190 , 188 ] . The deliberate pathway passes through conscious perception and planning and takes roughly 150 ms or more, the range of voluntary reaction times [ 188 ] . The reflex pathway is what vision cannot match, since even the fastest visual corrections take roughly 100 ms or more ( Section 4.2.5 ). 3.2.4 The brain predicts touch and acts on the discrepancy Why can you not tickle yourself? Because the brain predicts how your own action will feel: a copy of every motor command is used to forecast the touch it should produce [ 44 , 412 , 112 ] . The difference between predicted and actual touch is the control signal: either the prediction was off or the execution fell short. It serves two purposes at once. It triggers a correction of the action in progress [ 187 ] , and it updates the predictor, a role attributed to the cerebellum [ 413 ] , so the next lift starts with nearly correct grip forces. We return to the cerebellum, and to what it shares with a robot world model, in Section 5.2 . 3.2.5 Descending control suppresses predictable and irrelevant tactile channels Figure 9: Descending signals from cortex turn down predicted or irrelevant tactile channels and turn up the task-relevant one, so the fingertip signal arrives at high contrast. Prediction and attention together decide what the tactile system transmits. The skin streams signals constantly (clothes, watchband, chair), yet by a textbook estimate, of roughly 10 6 10^{6} bits/s entering the nerves only about five bits/s reach perception [ 456 ] . The selection is top-down: descending signals set the gain at each relay, turning down channels that prediction marks as expected, such as touch from your own movement, or that attention marks as irrelevant, and turning up the relevant one [ 61 , 377 , 411 ] . Filtering this early spares downstream spikes, which are costly [ 20 , 231 ] , and delivers the attended contact to cortex at high signal-to-noise ( Figure 9 ). 3.3 Inspiration Touch should measure the contact force that compliance control needs ( Section 3.3.1 ), reveal the physical properties of objects ( Section 3.3.2 ), and gather evidence actively with small probes ( Section 3.3.3 ). 3.3.1 Represent touch as a force field first, and let it drive compliance control We propose that touch enter the model as a force field: a contact force per point on the skin, with normal and shear components. Most sensor families can be calibrated to this form, at least approximately [ 441 , 37 ] , so data from different sensors pool directly and one embedding serves them all, where cross-sensor encoders must first learn a shared latent space [ 108 , 305 ] . The force field keeps only force and discards texture, vibration, and temperature. Raw signals keep all of these and also work [ 155 , 288 ] , but each sensor then needs its own tokenizer and enough data to train it. The model uses that representation in two ways, both through the contact force in strength and direction. Against a fragile or soft object, the strength decides when to stop closing; against a hard surface, the direction marks the axis to yield along, the compliance rule of Section 2.3.2 . Either form of the model’s action plan can apply it ( Section 6.3.3 ): as code, the model writes the rule, yield along the sensed normal and stop at a force threshold [ 239 ] ; as a reactive policy head, the head takes the tactile tokens as input and corrects the trajectory at the control rate. 3.3.2 Train the model to predict the tactile consequence of each command Given past observations and a new command, the model should predict the sensory consequence [ 156 , 249 , 443 ] : if past touch suggested high friction, how far the object slides under a given push; if it suggested a soft sponge, how much the sponge deforms under a given grip. This forces the model to infer the properties that geometry [ 304 , 206 ] leaves out and contact measures directly: mass, friction, compliance, and fragility, on which grip force and the risk of slip or breakage depend [ 432 , 227 ] . We train on exactly such data: the robot’s own executed actions, command as question and tactile outcome as answer, free of annotation, through the force-field calibration of Section 3.3.1 so one model serves every sensor. The same prediction pays off at run time. Once the real touch arrives, the model compares it with what it expected and acts on the difference, as the brain does ( Section 3.2.4 ). A grip that slips or a surface that gives more than predicted shows up as a mismatch at the first contact, and the sign and size of that mismatch say which action compensates: tighten the grip, ease the press. 3.3.3 Probe actively to test hypotheses about properties that cannot be seen When the property that matters cannot be seen, the robot should create the evidence before committing: lift the object a few millimeters to estimate load, tilt it to feel whether anything shifts inside, or press gently to measure stiffness, and let the outcome set the following strategy ( Figure 10 ) [ 45 , 227 ] . Probes should be uncertainty-driven, choosing the contact where competing hypotheses predict different outcomes [ 258 , 110 , 133 ] . The same probes are the cheapest self-improvement data: each is an action with a measured consequence, so it trains the model’s expectation of what its actions will do, data that passive demonstrations rarely contain ( Section 5.3.1 ) [ 127 , 316 ] . Figure 10: When an object’s properties cannot be seen, the robot should probe before it commits. Lifting, tilting, and pressing within safe bounds each test a hypothesis the camera cannot settle. 4 Vision Figure 11: The same ball is read twice, by the two visual streams in the brain. The ventral stream resolves its pattern and identity; the dorsal stream resolves its trajectory and guides the catch. Robotics borrows its vision encoders from computer vision, where they were optimized for object recognition and for image or video generation. An agent acting on an object does not need every detail of it at every instant; it needs where the object is, how it moves, and how to take hold of it. Biology runs two parallel “vision encoders” ( Figure 11 ): a slow one for fine detail and recognition, and a fast one dedicated to guiding motor behavior. Current encoders resemble the first, and the second has no counterpart. We first survey what current encoders were built for ( Section 4.1 ), then turn to how the brain builds a second visual system for motor behavior ( Section 4.2 ), and finally draw the algorithmic inspirations ( Section 4.3 ). 4.1 Robotics We review the training objective for current vision encoders ( Section 4.1.1 ), how the backbone behind them reshapes their tokens ( Section 4.1.2 ), and the limits that follow ( Section 4.1.3 ). 4.1.1 The pretraining objective decides what the tokens keep Almost all tokenizers are ViTs [ 94 ] pretrained at scale and then frozen or lightly fine-tuned; what distinguishes them is the pretraining objective, which leaves a durable fingerprint on the representation. Nearly every recipe asks for one of two things: predict the image or video itself , in pixels or in an embedding of it, or align it with a text description . Self-supervised encoders predict the input, in pixel space or in latent space. The recipes differ mainly in where the prediction target lives. Masked pixel reconstruction puts it in pixel space: the model repaints masked patches directly [ 151 , 419 , 27 , 380 ] . Masked latent prediction instead forecasts an exponential-moving-average teacher’s embeddings of the masked regions [ 17 ] ; on video this recovers motion and temporal structure without paying for pixel fidelity [ 28 , 18 ] . View-invariant self-distillation targets the teacher’s embedding of a different augmented view of the same image, with centering and sharpening to prevent collapse [ 55 , 299 , 359 ] ; correspondence, segmentation, and depth emerge in frozen probes. Caption alignment buys semantics but never asks for geometry. Image–text contrastive learning predicts which caption belongs to which image, pulling matched pairs together in a joint embedding space [ 325 , 445 , 385 ] . Because language alignment is the objective itself, these encoders became the vision towers of VLMs and, through them, of most VLAs. The cost is inherited from the captions: they rarely mention exact pose, contact, or metric layout, so nothing in the objective pressures the encoder to represent geometry. 4.1.2 The VLM or video world-model backbone acts as an extended vision encoder The backbone that consumes the tokens decides what the action head finally reads. In a VLA, image tokens enter the language model through a projector; the action head then reads its hidden states or key-value cache [ 42 , 40 ] , or the language model emits the action tokens itself [ 210 ] , so vision arrives fused with the instruction and the backbone’s semantic knowledge. World Action Models replace the language model with a video-diffusion backbone, so the action head reads features shaped by predicting scene change ( Section 5.1.1 ) [ 168 , 431 , 101 ] . Smaller imitation policies feed encoder features straight to the action head [ 70 , 450 , 102 ] . In every case, recognition, language, or generation shaped the representation, and none of them is control. 4.1.3 Current vision stacks are slow, blind to velocity, and miss fine detail Policies act on one stale observation for up to seconds. Cameras deliver 30–60 frames per second. Autoregressive VLAs typically infer at a few hertz [ 49 , 210 ] , and even the fastest flow-matching VLAs, which infer in tens of milliseconds [ 42 , 257 ] , still commit half a second to two seconds of motion to one observation and execute it blind [ 370 ] .
